title: The modern masters of deception
summary: De Hory, Myatt and Drewe, Beltracchi, the Knoedler 'Rothkos' and Mark Landis: five methods, five weak points.

shots.title:
The modern
masters.
shots.subtitle: Five forgers, five weak points.
shots.narration: Every forger has a method and a weak point. Here are five who fooled the experts within living memory — and how each was caught.
Elmyr de Hory posed as a dispossessed Hungarian aristocrat. With the dealer Fernand Legros he sold fakes on five continents, until 1967, when forty sold to one Texas collector were exposed.

shots.text: Old canvases scraped down. Fake **expert stamps**. Photos slipped into catalogues.
shots.narration: De Hory scraped flea-market paintings down to the primer. Legros forged experts' certification stamps and slipped photographs of the fakes into auction catalogues and monographs.
In Britain, John Drewe went further. Posing as a collector, he got into museum archives and altered the records, so that John Myatt's fakes acquired a documented past.

shots.text: House paint, lubricating jelly, coffee grounds, vacuum dust.
shots.narration: Myatt's materials were absurdly modern: household paint thickened with lubricating jelly, aged with coffee grounds and vacuum-cleaner dust. The paperwork did the convincing.

shots.label: Myatt fakes thought to be **still circulating**
shots.context: Of more than 200 made over seven years. Drewe got six years; Myatt one.
shots.narration: After a 1999 trial, Drewe received six years and Myatt one. Of more than two hundred fakes, about 120 are thought to be still circulating.

shots.text: **Beltracchi** painted the lost works in the catalogues.
shots.narration: Wolfgang Beltracchi filled gaps. He painted pictures recorded in old catalogues but long lost, and gave them labels from a collection that never existed.
A 'Campendonk' signed 1914 sold for 2.88 million euros in 2006. The laboratory then found titanium white of a kind made only from 1937. In 2011 Beltracchi was sentenced to six years.

shots.text: More than **60** fakes. Buyers paid over **80 million dollars**.
shots.narration: In New York, the dealer Glafira Rosales sold more than sixty never-exhibited 'Pollocks', 'Rothkos' and 'Motherwells' to two galleries. Buyers paid them over eighty million dollars.

shots.text: One painter in Queens. A Swiss client **who never existed**.
shots.narration: All were painted by one man in Queens. The provenance was an anonymous Swiss client who never existed. Knoedler, one of New York's oldest galleries, closed in 2011.
And Mark Landis? For thirty years he gave fakes away to museums, posing as a philanthropist. Because nobody paid him, he technically committed no fraud.

steps.brief: Each trick below comes from a real case. Did it fake the object's materials and age, or the documents and story around it?

options: Titanium white of a kind industrially made only from 1937/38
questions.explain: The Doerner Institut found rutile titanium white in two layers.

questions.prompt: Why did Drewe and Myatt's scheme work despite unconvincing paintings?
options: Drewe planted false records in archives that experts trust
questions.explain: The forged paper trail made weak paintings look documented.

questions.prompt: Why was Mark Landis never convicted of fraud?
options: He gave the works away and claimed no tax deductions
questions.explain: With no payment and no financial loss, there was technically no fraud.

questions.prompt: In the Knoedler case, what provenance did the dealer offer?
options: An anonymous Swiss client — who never existed
questions.explain: She also claimed a Spanish collector who never owned the works.
